De novo Design of Protein Switches with Diffusion-Based Ensemble Sampling

1. Diff-Switch reframes protein switch design as controlled ensemble generation: instead of designing a single backbone, it samples a backbone ensemble where each domain stays locally close to a reference structure while global domain arrangements diversify along a user-chosen switching coordinate.

2. Core technical idea: combine reward-tilted sampling from a pretrained protein backbone diffusion model with a metadynamics-inspired, history-dependent bias in collective-variable (CV) space to avoid repeatedly sampling the same global arrangement.

3. The method starts from one known conformation xref plus a domain decomposition. A local similarity reward penalizes per-domain deviation from xref (e.g., sum of per-domain RMSDs after rigid alignment), preserving domain geometry while allowing inter-domain motion.

4. To explicitly drive exploration of alternative states, Diff-Switch adds well-tempered metadynamics in CV space (e.g., domain center-of-mass distance). Gaussian “hills” are deposited where the sampler has already visited, flattening barriers and encouraging discovery of new global arrangements.

5. Implementation detail: sampling uses Twisted Diffusion Sampler (TDS), a sequential Monte Carlo method for diffusion inference-time control that targets the reward-tilted distribution and becomes asymptotically exact as particle count increases.

6. Practical output: after K iterations, all sampled backbones are pooled into an ensemble E, and an alternative state xalt is selected as the most dissimilar member to xref under the chosen dissimilarity metric. The pair {xref, xalt} is then sent to multi-state inverse folding (ProteinMPNN-MSD / Caliby) to design a single sequence compatible with both states.

7. Benchmark (20 two-state domain-motion proteins, 109–801 aa): using Diff-Switch-generated conformations as inputs to multi-state sequence design improves the success rate of finding switch-compatible sequences over a baseline that designs from a single conformation.

8. Quantitatively, across reference-state choices (open vs closed) and inverse-folding backends (ProteinMPNN vs Caliby), Diff-Switch increases AUC of success-rate curves by ~0.09–0.17, with significant improvements by paired Wilcoxon tests across proteins for both scRMSDswitch and scTMswitch metrics.

9. Realistic case study: phosphorylation-induced switching where only a closed state is given. Using a CV tied to the trigger (distance between a phosphorylation-site helix and scaffold), Diff-Switch generates candidate open conformations automatically, avoiding manual “open-state construction” used in prior work; 25% (4/16) designed sequences show phosphorylation-dependent opening by AF3, vs 0/16 for baseline.

10. Limitations are explicit: performance depends on choosing a CV that matches the true motion (e.g., center-of-mass distance fails for pure rotations), and the current formulation mainly targets rigid/semi-rigid domain rearrangements rather than fold-changing transitions; future work includes better CV discovery and broader trigger mechanisms.

RLHF by hand ✍️ ~ 15 steps walkthrough below

Train a model on human text and it inherits human bias. It will assume a doctor is a "him", because the data says so.

RLHF is the correction. A human marks one preference, doc is them over doc is him, and the weights move.

But one correction is not the point. The hope is that the model learns the value behind it, gender neutrality, and applies it to professions nobody ever mentioned.

How does it work?

Goal: train a reward model from a single human comparison about doctors, then turn it on CEOs, filling in every cell yourself.

= 1. Given =

A reward model, an LLM, and two (prompt, next) pairs.

= 2. Preferences =

A human reads both pairs and picks a winner: (doc is, them) beats (doc is, him). The loser is not bad grammar, it is gender bias, and that is the whole signal.

= 3. Word embeddings =

Let us look up each word of the loser pair. These vectors are the reward model's input.

= 4. Linear layer =

We multiply by the reward model's weights and add its biases. Out come feature vectors, one per position.

= 5. Mean pool =

Let us multiply by [1/3, 1/3, 1/3], which averages the three positions into one sentence embedding.

= 6. Output layer =

We map that sentence down to a single number. Reward = 3.

= 7. The winner, the same way =

Let us repeat steps 3 to 6 on the winning pair. Reward = 5.

= 8. Winner minus loser =

We take the gap: 5 - 3 = 2. The reward model wants this positive and as large as it can make it.

= 9. Loss gradient =

Let us squash the gap into a probability, σ(2) ≈ 0.9, and subtract the target of 1. The gradient is -0.1, and it goes back through the purple weights. The reward model is now trained.

= 10. A prompt it has never seen =

We start the second half with "[S] CEO is". The feedback in step 2 was about doctors. Nothing connects a CEO to a doctor except what the reward model generalised.

= 11. Transformer =

Let us push it through attention and a feed forward layer, one vector per position.

= 12. Output probabilities =

We map each vector to a score over the vocabulary.

= 13. Sample =

Let us take the highest score. The model completes "CEO is" with "him", which is the same bias the human penalised in step 2.

= 14. Score it with the reward model =

We feed the new pair (CEO is, him) through steps 3 to 6. Reward = 3, exactly the score it gave "doc is him" in step 6. Nobody taught it about CEOs. The value transferred.

= 15. Loss gradient =

Let us set the loss to the negative of the reward, so minimising the loss maximises the reward. The gradient is a constant -1, and it goes back through the red weights.

The outputs:
Loser reward = 3, winner reward = 5
Reward gap = 2, predicted σ ≈ 0.9, reward model gradient = -0.1
LLM samples "him", reward = 3, LLM gradient = -1

Congrats! You just calculated RLHF by hand.

And you watched a value generalise: one comparison about doctors, and the model marks down "CEO is him" unprompted.

whoever leaked this has bigger balls than sense

two researchers replaced $7,500 of human grading with $77.81 of model calls, and the number that fell out should stop anyone shipping an agent this week: the judge disagrees with itself 13.6% of the time

it also prefers whichever answer it saw first, 72% of the time. cross-judge agreement is a kappa of 0.51: the statistical polite word for guessing

this is Eval Engineering, the layer that arrives after loops and graphs, and it installs into the agent you already pay for:

- run every comparison both ways and average the two, because one production judge picked whichever answer sat in the first slot 72% of the time
- stop shipping on a single verdict: recovering the reference answer took 11 repeated trials before a majority vote landed it, and 15 on the questions that actually mattered
- report the chance-corrected agreement instead of raw match, since the gap between those two ran 33 to 41 points on the same benchmark
- never let a model grade its own family, because self-preference tracks capability upward rather than falling away as models improve
- test stability and bias together, since two judges already running in production held above 0.95 on repeat while carrying severe positional preference
- freeze the rubric wording and version it, because semantically identical templates flipped the majority outcome in a quarter of tested cases
- write the rubric as one observable pass condition rather than a bundle of scores, so a coin-flip preference cannot hide inside an average
- let plain code take every objective call, did the test pass, does the file exist, did the state change, and leave the judge only what genuinely needs reading
- make the verdict do something structural to the run in flight, reject the handoff, swap the node, quarantine the branch, or you have built a dashboard

the catch is that your judge is a measurement instrument nobody calibrates: single-trial judging is too noisy for anything you would stake money on, and the same judges reordered by as much as 14 positions depending on which benchmark you asked

so the loop has to converge on the spec rather than on the score, because optimise against a judge long enough and the agent learns to look right instead of being right

Which AI Model To Use? Stop Using ChatGPT For Everything - Use This Cheat Sheet

99% use ChatGPT for everything. Pros pick the right model for the right job. Here is the exact map:

01. General Chat and Productivity
Best: ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Pi (Inflection AI)
For daily chat, emails, productivity. Fast and human.

02. Advanced Reasoning and Problem Solving
Best: Claude, Deepseek, Gemini, Yi-34B, Mistral
For complex logic, math, strategy. Claude and Deepseek lead here.

03. Coding and Developer Tasks
Best: Github Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, StarCoder2

Copilot for in-IDE, Claude for full codebase reasoning, StarCoder2 for open-source coding.

04. Creative Writing and Ideation
Best: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Mistral
Claude = best human voice, ChatGPT = most versatile, Mistral = creative edge.

05. Search, Research and Web Knowledge
Best: Perplexity, ChatGPT, Grok, You com
Perplexity is #1 for cited research. Grok and You. com for real-time web.

06. Long Document and Data Analysis
Best: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Deepseek, Yi-34B
Claude 200K context window king, Gemini 1M for massive docs.

07. Multi-modal Tasks (Image, Audio, Text)
Best: ChatGPT, Gemini, InternLM2, Claude, Grok
Gemini and GPT-4o for vision + audio + text in one flow.

08. Open-Source or Self-Hosted Options
Best: Deepseek, Yi-34B, Mistral, StarCoder2, GPT4All
Run private, offline, no data leaving. Deepseek and Mistral are best.

09. Enterprise and Secure Use
Best: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, LM Studio
For teams, SSO, compliance. LM Studio for local private enterprise.

10. Education and Tutoring
Best: ChatGPT, Deepseek, Claude, Perplexity
Best explainers. Perplexity for cited learning, Claude for Socratic tutoring.
Stop using one model for 10 jobs. Use the right tool, get 10x better output.

Machine verifiable reward is a proxy for "useful to a human" and a model optimises the proxy it is handed rather than the one you meant. So this is not an alignment failure but it is alignment doing exactly what you specified, toward a cheaper target.

Human preference is costly to measure but checkable correctness is nearly free and optimization drains toward whatever is cheapest to score.
